en: The Sūtra on the Lion’s Roar of the Elder’s Daughter Ātreyī Spoken by the Buddha;
the translator’s name is lost, now appended to the Liang Dynasty Record.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with an immeasurable assembly of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, and bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
At that time, more than twenty li to the west of the city of Śrāvastī, there was a village named Daṇḍaka.
A brāhmaṇa named Vāsiṣṭha lived therein; he was widely learned in various fields of study, possessed deep faith in the inner scriptures, and reverently upheld the Buddha’s teachings.
At that time, a brahmin wished to convene a great assembly; he went to the Jeta Grove and invited the Buddha and the Sangha. The Buddha accepted his invitation, and the brahmin returned home.
Furthermore, at that appointed time, the Buddha, together with the great assembly, went to that village and arrived at the house of the brahmin.

At that moment, the elder saw the Buddha and was so overcome with joy and exultation that he could not contain himself; he immediately led his kinsmen and followers to where the Buddha was, and each paid homage to the Buddha before standing respectfully before him.
That brahmin had an eldest daughter named Āṭikā, who had previously been given in marriage to another man but had returned home for a short time to attend to her parents.

The girl was of upright appearance and noble character; she was gentle and humble in her conduct, possessed a broad and open mind, and was able to harmonize relations between husband and wife. She served her kin with devotion and attended to her husband as if he were a deity; her deportment was peerless, surpassing that of all others.
The parents and their retinue all went out to see the Buddha, but this daughter alone remained inside the room.
Because her parents had been unable to fathom the origins of her birth from the time she was born, they named her Āṭavikā.
At that time, the Tathāgata immediately knew that the elder had a daughter who remained inside the room and had not yet come forth; he also knew the reason why she did not emerge.
Had she emerged, she would have brought benefit to immeasurable multitudes, as well as to all devas and humans.
The Buddha then addressed the elder, saying, "Have all your kinsmen come forth?
The brahmin stood with his hands bound, kneeling before the Buddha; because of the girl's failure to emerge, he felt ashamed and remained silent, offering no reply.
The Buddha, knowing her thoughts, addressed her, saying, "The time for the midday meal is approaching; may you prepare the offerings?

Thereupon, the brahmin followed the Buddha’s instruction and began to set out the offerings. When the great assembly, as well as the elder and his retinue, had finished their midday meal, only this girl had not yet received food.
At that time, the Tathāgata intentionally left some food remaining in his alms bowl and sent a manifested woman to take this leftover food and give it to the woman Āmrapālī within that room.
Then the manifested woman addressed her with a verse, saying:
"This is the remainder of the Tathāgata, Bestowed by the Unsurpassed and Most Victorious Honored One."
"I shall follow the Buddha's teaching; may you, O virtuous one, accept it with purity.
Then the maiden Āmrapālī praised him in verse, saying: "Alas!"
"O Great Compassionate One, knowing that I am in this chamber, you have now granted me this single-flavored food; I now look up in reverence at your holy intent.
He then replied to that transformed woman with a verse:
"I constantly contemplate what I have longed for: the conduct of the Great Sage."
"I have never been different from you; why is it that you are not pure?
Having heard this verse spoken by Āṭavikā, the emanated woman immediately vanished and disappeared.
The woman Ātichā recited these verses from her heart:
“Where is my husband now?
I pray he will come forth to see the Supreme Honored One. May he know the purity of my heart; may he come quickly so that we may hear the teaching together.”
At that time, by the power of Anticchā’s pure mind, her husband arrived at her side as soon as he thought of her.
Upon seeing her husband, the woman Anticchā was filled with joy and praised him in verse, saying: "O!..."
"O Great and Victorious Honored One, you have now fulfilled my wish; I do not regret breaking a minor precept, for I fear we shall no longer hear [the Dharma] together.
When her husband saw Āṭavikā having spoken this verse, he immediately rebuked her in return with a verse, saying: "Alas!"
"You are greatly deluded, not knowing what is appropriate for yourself. You have caused the Sage to labor by offering him leftover food; what is the point of observing the precepts?
At that time, the woman Āṭīśā followed her husband to the place where the Buddha was, and each paid homage to the Buddha and the great assembly, standing respectfully before them.
Then the woman Āṭīcā praised him in verse:
"I call to mind the Great Compassionate One, The Honored One who protects the ten directions;
I wish to offer you this secret treasury, So please grant me the remains of your pure food."
"The Great Sage is most difficult to encounter; the minds of the world harbor doubts.
Who can be asked about the Dharma to establish the foundation for the various bodhicittas?
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One! Who is this woman?
How is it that she has suddenly come here and spoken such verses of Dharma, saying that she has obtained leftover food?”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"This is the daughter of the householder. He asked again:
"From where have you come?
For what reason have you arrived here?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"This woman has not come from afar; she resides only in this chamber.

Although she has parents and kinsmen, her husband is absent. Because she restrains herself out of reverence and obedience toward her husband, she does not leave her parents' home lightly to appear before the great assembly."
Then Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By what virtuous cause has this girl been born into the family of this elder, and why is her appearance such as this?
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions has she obtained such a husband who restricts her so severely that she cannot freely see the Buddha and the Saṅgha?"
The Buddha then said to Śāriputra,
"Ask her yourself. Thereupon,
Śāriputra questioned the girl, saying:
“By what causes and conditions were you born into this householder’s family?
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions did you obtain such a man as your husband, who imposes such prohibitions that you are unable to see the Buddha and the Sangha at will?”
The woman Āṭavikā replied in verse:
“Born without ill repute into this householder’s family,
and not clinging to the notion of being a woman, I have obtained such a pure husband.”
While within my inner chamber, I thought I had attained ultimate mastery;
yet this portion has never been transcended—what the Noble One knows has been granted to me as a remainder. Alas!
Now, O Great Virtuous One, you do not know the source of reality; because you do not deviate from it by even a hair’s breadth, you are named Mahāvaśavartin.
Although I am within your inner chamber, you honor me as if I were manifest before your eyes;
yet though you call yourself an Arhat, you constantly follow me and cannot see me.
The Great Sage is not form, yet he does not exist apart from the physical body;
when the śrāvakas saw Pāpīyas, they thought it was a man of great power. Alas!
"Now, O Virtuous One, following the Sage with limited skillful means, you do not know the fundamental origin and have conceived a perverted view toward me.
At that time, Śāriputra fell silent and ceased speaking, thinking privately to himself:
"What kind of woman is this?"
"His eloquence is such as this, which is beyond my reach.
The Buddha, immediately perceiving his thoughts, addressed him, saying:
"Do not retreat from this dialogue, nor give rise to a contrary mind."
"This woman has already encountered immeasurable Buddhas; do not doubt the Dharma-medicine she has spoken.
At that time, Mañjuśrī asked Ātreyikā, "Do you now understand the meaning of birth and death?"
He replied, "I know it by the power of the Buddha. He asked again:
"If one knows this, what is the meaning of 'arising'?
He replied: "The meaning of arising is arising through non-arising."
He asked again:
"In what sense does 'non-arising' constitute the meaning of arising? He replied:

"If one can clearly know that the four conditions of earth, water, fire, and wind have never, in the ultimate sense, attained any state of combination, yet can speak according to what is appropriate to the circumstances, this constitutes the meaning of 'arising.'"
He asked again:

"If one knows that earth, water, fire, and wind ultimately cannot be found to combine with one another to constitute the meaning of 'arising,' then there would be no characteristic of arising; what, then, would serve as its meaning?"
He replied: "To be in the place of birth yet to be without birth is what constitutes true birth;
therefore, it is said that there is meaning. Mañjuśrī asked again:
"What is the meaning of death? He replied,
"The meaning of death is dying by means of non-death."
He asked again:
"In what sense is 'not dying' considered the meaning of death? He replied:
"If one can clearly know that earth, water, fire, and wind ultimately cannot be found as anything that disperses, yet is able to speak according to what is appropriate, this is the meaning of death."
He asked again:
"If one knows that earth, water, fire, and wind ultimately cannot be found as something that disperses, then there would be no sign of death; what, then, would constitute its meaning?"
He replied: "Though one is in the place of death, if the mind does not perish, this constitutes true death;
therefore, it is said that there is meaning. Mañjuśrī asked again:
"What is the meaning of 'permanence'? He replied:

"If one can clearly understand that all phenomena are ultimately subject to arising, ceasing, and transformation, and that they lack fixed nature like the appearance of an illusion, yet can speak according to what is appropriate for each situation—this is the meaning of permanence."
He asked again:

"If one knows that all phenomena are ultimately subject to arising and ceasing, lacking any fixed nature, and possessing a character like an illusion—this is precisely the meaning of impermanence; how can it be taken as the meaning of permanence?"

He replied: "All phenomena arise without attaining arising, and cease without attaining cessation; even their transformation is likewise so. Because they do not attain [these states], they are said to have the meaning of permanence."
He asked again: "What is the meaning of impermanence? He replied:

"If one knows that all phenomena are ultimately neither born nor extinguished, and can accordingly speak as is appropriate in accordance with such characteristics, this is the meaning of impermanence."
He asked again:
"If one knows that all phenomena are ultimately neither born nor extinguished, this is the meaning of permanence; why then do you speak of it as the meaning of impermanence?"

He replied: "It is simply because all phenomena are subject to sovereign transformation and lack fixed characteristics, and do not attain independence; knowing them thus, one speaks of the meaning of impermanence."
He asked again: "What is the meaning of emptiness? He replied:

"If one can know the characteristics of all phenomena such that they have never been self-empty, yet do not destroy their present existence, and is thus able to neither empty the empty nor affirm the existent, then one speaks of the meaning of the existence of emptiness."
He asked again:
"If there is neither 'emptiness of emptiness' nor 'existence of existence,' then there would be no objective reality;
what, then, would constitute the meaning of emptiness? The woman Āmrapālī replied with a verse:
“Alas! You who possess true great virtue, yet do not understand the meaning of true emptiness: form has no intrinsic nature; is it not, indeed, like space?”
"If emptiness were inherently empty, it would be unable to contain form;
because emptiness is not empty of itself, all forms arise from it.
At that time, Mañjuśrī asked again:
"Is there anyone who clearly knows that birth is characterized by non-birth, yet is detained by birth?
He replied: "There is.
It refers to one who, although clearly sees this for himself, lacks sufficient power and is thus detained by birth."
He asked again:
"Is there anyone who, being ignorant and unaware of the nature of birth, is ultimately not detained by birth? He replied:

"No! Why is this? If one does not perceive the nature of arising, then although one may attain a slight state of peace through discipline, the characteristic of unrest will constantly serve as its counteragent."
If one can perceive the nature of arising, then even while dwelling in a state of insecurity, auspicious signs will constantly manifest before them.
If one does not understand it in this way, then although one may possess various superior eloquences and discourse upon profound scriptures, this is merely the mind of arising and ceasing.

To speak of the secret essentials regarding their true nature is like a blind person describing colors; because they rely on the words of others, they can say that there are blue, yellow, red, white, and black, yet they cannot see the actual characteristics of color themselves.
Those who currently cannot perceive all phenomena are likewise in this same situation.
However, that which is currently born is destined for death; as for that which has died, for that person there is no longer any meaning of birth or death.
It is the same for those who are bound by the notions of permanence or impermanence.
"You should know, Venerable One!
Even emptiness does not itself attain emptiness; therefore, it is said that there is the meaning of emptiness.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī:
"So it is, so it is! Just as Aṇḍhaka has spoken, it is true and not otherwise.
The sun might be made cold and the moon might be made hot, but what Aṇḍhaka has spoken cannot be altered."
Then Śāriputra again asked the girl:
"Since your wisdom and eloquence are such as these—praised by the Buddha and beyond the reach of us śrāvakas—why are you unable to leave behind this female body and its physical characteristics?"
The girl replied: "I wish to question the Venerable One; please answer me as you see fit.
Venerable One!"
"Are you currently a man? Śāriputra replied,
"Although my form is that of a man, my mind is not that of a man."
The girl said, "Venerable Sir! I am also like this;
as you have said, although I possess the physical form of a woman, my mind is not that of a woman."
Śāriputra said, "You are currently being held captive by your husband; how can you act like this?
The woman replied:
"Venerable One!
Are you able to have confidence in what you yourself have said? Śāriputra replied:
"How can my own words not be self-confident? The woman replied, "If you are self-confident,
then regarding what the Venerable One previously stated— that 'my physical form is male, but my mind is not male'— this implies that the mind and the physical form have two distinct functions."
If you, Venerable One, have confidence in these words, you will not give rise to the evil view that I am a husband.
Since you are yourself a man, you perceive me as a woman; because of my female form, your mind is corrupted.
However, one who perceives her as a woman while being himself a man cannot give rise to true faith in the Dharma.
Śāriputra said, "I do not dare to give rise to an evil view regarding you. The girl replied:
"It is only because of my reverence for the World-Honored One that I did not dare speak the truth.
If I truly had not conceived such an evil view, why would you say, 'You are now currently held captive by your husband'?"
"From where do these words come?
Śāriputra replied, "Because I have long been free from habitual tendencies, these words arise; they do not stem from my true mind."
The woman asked: "Venerable sir!
Please answer me as you please regarding what I have now asked."
"Venerable sir, since you say that you have long been free from the marks of male and female, has your physical form long been free [from them],
or is it your mind? At this, Śāriputra remained silent and did not answer.
At that time, Āṭavikā spoke in verse:
"If the mind has long been detached, And ultimately no views arise,
who would act as a woman To give rise to impurity toward form?"
If one considers that form has long since departed, and phenomena are fundamentally not of their own accord,
being ultimately never defiled— what then could one use to commit evil? Alas!
Now, O Virtuous Ones, you may study in vain yet remain unable to know; that I call a male "male" and a female "female"—is this not a false conceptualization?
I repent of my transgression before the great assembly; do not harbor doubts regarding the Dharma.
What I have spoken above is sustained by the Buddha’s spiritual power.
When Āṭavika had spoken these verses, more than one thousand people—monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen, devas, and humans—attained the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

There was an assembly of five thousand, among whom some attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), some attained the Dharma-eye, and others attained liberation through the mind; furthermore, there were immeasurable śrāvaka followers who felt a sense of self-reproach regarding the Buddha’s teaching.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra:

"This woman is no ordinary person; she has already encountered immeasurable Buddhas and is constantly able to preach such a definitive sūtra of the lion’s roar, benefiting immeasurable sentient beings."
I, too, have already practiced together with this woman under immeasurable Buddhas; before long, this woman shall attain perfect enlightenment.

Among this assembly, those who are able to give rise to true faith in the essential Dharma taught by this woman do so because they have long heard the Dharma she has taught, and thus are now able to give rise to right faith.
"Therefore, you should receive this *Sīhanāda-nītārtha-sūtra* with careful attention and harbor no doubts.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda, saying:

"You should receive and uphold these verses and sequential passages from the *Sīhanāda-nītārtha-praśnavyākaraṇa-sūtra* concerning the daughter of the elder, Aṅgulimālā; I entrust them to you, and you should receive them with careful attention."
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"So be it, World-Honored One!
I have now received them all."

At that time, having heard the Dharma taught by the woman Ātichā, the great assembly was filled with immense joy; their hearts leaped with immeasurable delight, and each person practiced according to what had been taught.
The Sūtra on the Lion’s Roar of the Meaning of Ultimate Truth Spoken by the Buddha to the Elder’s Daughter Ātīcā.
